title: Having data isn't enough. You have to know how to tell the story
description: Data alone doesn't convince anyone. How to turn numbers into a story that leads to a decision, and why visualization is UX too.

related.title: Clint Acquire
related.body: In practice: a landing page and a conversational flow that captured 79% of the sales demand.

blocks.text: One of the things that most changed the way I think about product was realizing that data, on its own, doesn't convince anyone.

items: We can have a dashboard full of numbers
We can present a conversion rate
We can show a growth chart

blocks.text: But there's still one question:
What is this data trying to tell us?
That's where narrative comes in.
A number is not a story
Imagine presenting:

steps.label: What are we going to do?

blocks.caption: The structure of a good data story ends in a decision.

data.b: But what should we do with it?
data.story: “Conversion dropped from 6.1% to 4.2% after the form change. The drop happens mainly on mobile, where the second field has the highest abandonment rate.”
data.f: That makes a product conversation much easier.

blocks.text: Data visualization is UX too
When we build a dashboard, we're building an interface.
There's a person on the other side trying to understand something.

items: They need to spot what matters

blocks.text: That's why a visualization has to answer a need.
Ten charts are useless if none of them helps anyone make a decision.
Sometimes a single, well-chosen chart says more than an entire page.
What happened?

items.q: How will we know it worked?

data.close: This sequence turns a report into a product conversation.

blocks.text: Data and storytelling are not separate things
When we talk about data storytelling, we're not talking about making up a story to make the number look prettier.
It's the opposite.
It's organizing the data so the important information becomes clearer.
For example:
Instead of showing 12 metrics all highlighted equally, we can show:
Main change
Possible cause
Impact
Next step
That helps the team move from reading to deciding.
Product Designers need to tell stories too
This skill shows up at many moments.
When we explain a decision to stakeholders.
It's not enough to say what we did.
We need to explain:
What was the problem?
What did we discover?
What did we decide?
Why did we decide that?
What happened next?
This structure makes the work much easier to understand.
Growth needs the same clarity

items: Growth works with lots of metrics

blocks.text: But a meeting full of metrics may lead to no decision at all.
The role of narrative is to help connect the dots.

data.chain: Traffic went up → but activation dropped → mainly in one specific channel → users arrive with a different expectation → we need to revisit the value proposition.
data.after: Now there's a direction to investigate.

blocks.text: The risk of looking only at the average
Another common problem is looking only at an overall metric.

blocks.caption: The 5% average looks stable. Segmented, it shows where conversion is suffering.

blocks.text: Imagine the average conversion is 5%.
It looks like just a number.
But maybe:
Now the average hides an important difference.
Segmentation can reveal the story.
And that can completely change the decision.
Data needs questions
We don't need to start with:
“What data do we have?”
We can start with:
“What do we want to understand?”
Then:
“What decision do we need to make?”
And only then:
“What data can help us?”
This inversion keeps us from building dashboards just because we have access to the data.
The designer's role in this conversation
Designers have an interesting advantage here.
We're used to organizing information.
All of that exists in data visualization too.
A chart needs hierarchy too.
A dashboard needs information architecture too.
A report needs a good reading experience too.
That's why data visualization can be a natural extension of Product Design work.
The best story is the one that leads to a decision
In the end, we don't need to create pretty presentations.
We need to help someone understand something important.
A good data narrative should make the person think:
“Now I get what's going on.”
And then:
“Now I know what we need to investigate or do.”
That's the point.
Because data doesn't create value just because it exists.
It creates value when it helps someone make a better decision.
